en: In the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, within the "Chapter on the True Wisdom of the Ācārya," there is the gate of the Ācārya’s meditation on the syllable *A*,

also known as the "Contemplation for Accomplishing the Body through the Fourfold Wheel of Syllables Maṇḍala," and also known as the "Contemplative Practice of the Triple Array of Syllables Maṇḍala for Accomplishing the Body."

Composed by the monk Weijin of the Five-Section Recitation Monks at Bijiqian in Jingying Monastery. *Cheng ruli gui yi* (The Ritual Manual for Entering into Principle), one fascicle. Now, as for the term "ācārya," it refers to the most secret among secrets within the exegesis [of the teachings]: the wisdom of mantras and the great mind.
The letter *A* is called the seed; therefore, all things are thus. According to the Dharma, one receives everything universally.

If, within this teaching, one understands this vast wisdom and the great merit of perfect enlightenment, such a person is called an *ācārya*; they are indeed the Tathāgata and are also named a Buddha.
In Sanskrit it is called *hanlida*; *hanlida* is the true mind, which is the syllable *A*.
Now, as for the syllable *A*, it is the mother of all Buddhas, the source from which all mantras arise, the most supreme and wondrous, the very character of the Buddha-mind.

If it is said that the internal sound of the syllable A is the sound from within the throat, one should know that this syllable A pervades all limbs and members; this is precisely the meaning of "primordial non-arising."
The term *brahman* has two pronunciations; one is *akṣara*, which is the root syllable and also signifies "immovable. This "immovable" refers to the meaning of *bodhicitta*.
Just as with the first two sounds, *a* and *ā*, which are the root letters;
the subsequent twelve characters, from *i* and *ī* up to *u* and *ū*, are all derivative and augmented characters, and they are all feminine vowels.
The fundamental syllable is masculine in tone; masculine tone has the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*), while feminine tone has the meaning of concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, it is explained that there are five tones:
the tone of the essence of the syllable *A*; [and so forth].
The syllable *A* is the sound of practice;
the twelve syllables from *I* and *Ī* to *O* and *Au* are all sounds of samādhi;
the syllable *Am* is the sound of realizing perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The syllable *aḥ* is the sound of entering Great Parinirvāṇa.
If one sees the syllables *ya*, *raṅ*, *ña*, *na*, or *maṅ*, they are identical to the vowel sign *u* (the dot above), which is also the sound of realizing *Tri-sambodhi*.
If one sees the eight syllables *ya*, *ra*, and so forth, they are identical to the consonant sign *i* (the dot to the side), which is also the sound of Great Parinirvāṇa.

The fundamental syllable pervades all places, and the augmented syllable also pervades all places; the fundamental and the augmented are not distinct from one another. Both take the body of the fundamental syllable as their basis, with additional strokes added to the sides and corners. Therefore, the fundamental and the augmented are neither identical nor different.

It is like water contained within a vessel; because of the vessel, the water is held, and the water does not leave the vessel. In this way, they mutually support one another, able to pervade both the internal and external.
It is not only the letter *A* that pervades all places; subsequently, from *Ka*, *Kha*, *Ga*, *Gha*, *Ṅa*, up to the conjunct letter *Kṣa*, these also pervade all places.
Why is this? Because they are all sounds of the fundamental [syllable], and that fundamental sound is the letter *A*.

Furthermore, as with the letter *Ka*, each has its own derivative and augmented characters; for instance, within the letter *Ka* there is the character *Ke* (計蓋), which is a feminine sound, formed by adding a stroke to the body of the letter *Ka* to create an augmented character.

Its essence is the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*), yet it is further characterized by the mutual support of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom; when these are unified as one, its essence is not lost, and the simultaneous practice of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) likewise pervades all places.
Thus, the augmentations pervade the roots, and the roots pervade the augmentations; the "arising from birth" pervades the seeds, and the seeds pervade the "arising from birth."
Therefore, in Sanskrit it is called "upabandha," which is also termed "initiation. It is like a seed producing fruit, and that fruit in turn becoming a seed.

Now, this letter A is identical to the seed; it can produce manifold fruits, each of which further produces hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions of times more, even extending through infinite and ineffable successions.
However, when one perceives the fruit through its cognition, since the cause is thus, one should know that the fruit must necessarily be like it.

This present letter *A* is also like this: from this fundamental, teacherless, spontaneous wisdom, all activities of omniscience arise and are distributed throughout the various branches. That which is distributed throughout the branches is precisely one's own mind; by means of this self-mind, all constituent parts are subsumed. Apart from the mind there is no body, and apart from the body there is no mind; this is likewise identical to the letter *A*.

If one pervades all with these syllables, one is identical to all Buddhas; that is to say, because the fruit arises from the syllables, one is a Buddha, and because one is able to realize perfect knowledge, one is called a Perfectly Awakened One (Samyaksambuddha).
Because one recognizes the rational nature of these syllables, one attains the name "Tathāgata.
The rational nature of these syllables refers to the meaning that this syllable *A* is precisely the principle of primordial non-arising.

Furthermore, just as a person possesses a mind that pervades all limbs and experiences both suffering and pleasure throughout them, so too does the letter A pervade all limbs; this is the meaning of the fundamental non-arising of the mind.
The letter *A* pervades all letters; if all letters were devoid of the letter *A*, they would not constitute letters at all—there must be the letter *A*.

If a letter lacks a head, it does not form a letter; therefore, the letter *A* serves as the head. From the sound of the single letter *A*, the sound of *A* exists within all sounds whatsoever. One who does not grasp this sound of *A* cannot understand how sound arises from the manifestation of phonemes. Because sound arises, and because sound exists, it pervades all constituent parts and is able to manifest all mundane and supramundane phenomena.

If one were to see only the phonetic characters, they could express the underlying principle; yet, it is further necessary for tones, language, teeth, and lips to have something to express—namely, categories of all phenomena such as blue, yellow, red, white;
east, west, south, north; square, round, large, small; above, below, noble, and humble—only then can they be fully understood. Thus, the Sūtra says: "O Guhyapati!..."
"This is the dharma-gate that pervades all places.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"These phonemes enable one to reach the further shore through wisdom regarding all mundane and supramundane skillful dharmas; various methods and diverse arts are mastered with nothing left out."
He accumulated profound understanding in the fields of writing and mathematics;
he was skilled in medical prescriptions and incantations for effectively curing all manner of ailments.

There were sentient beings possessed by malevolent spirits, those afflicted by the curses of enemies or hatred, those affected by the portents of evil stars, those pursued by wandering corpses, and those suffering from epilepsy, emaciation, and various other diseases—all of whom he was able to rescue and restore to full health.

Furthermore, he skillfully distinguishes and knows the origins of all treasures—gold, silver, pearls, shells, coral, lapis lazuli, mani-jewels, carnelian, kīṭasāra, and so forth—as well as their differing varieties and their respective values;

whether it be villages, camps, towns, small or large cities, palaces, gardens, groves, rocky springs, or marshes—in short, all places where people dwell—the Bodhisattva is able to provide protection and guidance according to each location.

Furthermore, he skillfully observes celestial phenomena and terrestrial geography, the auspiciousness or misfortune of human physiognomy, the cries of birds and beasts, the appearance of clouds and mists and seasonal climates, the abundance or scarcity of the year's harvests, and the security or peril of nations.
"In this way, there are no worldly arts and crafts that he has not mastered or thoroughly investigated to their very source.
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:
"O Lord of Mysteries!"
Therefore, the syllable *A* is taken as the head; the syllable *A* is the heart of the mantra, the very word of the Buddha’s mind.
What has been explained above—that the ācārya abides in the stage of Buddhahood—is still not fully understood; it refers precisely to this practice of the visualization-gate of the syllable *A*.
This syllable A is also called the wisdom of śamatha, it is also called the wisdom of vipaśyanā, it is also called the wisdom of the true jewel, and it is also called the wisdom of omniscience.
Therefore, a sutra states:

"All-knowledge, fundamental wisdom, and subsequently attained wisdom—arising from subsequently attained wisdom, great compassion arises; arising from great compassion, the three types of transformation bodies arise."

Now, if the ācārya contemplates these syllables and attains resonance with them, his own body is identical to the body of Vairocana Buddha; it is also called the indestructible vajra-body, the body that universally manifests in all forms, and the threefold mind-born body.

The Ācārya says: Contemplate this wheel of the letter A as being like the eye of a peacock’s tail, surrounded by radiance. When the practitioner dwells within it, they abide in the state of Buddhahood. Therefore, the letter A manifests within the mirror-like wisdom of the pure *dharmadhātu*. From this letter A, all other letters revolve and are produced; they pervade all names and mantras, circling and returning hundreds of thousands of millions of times. Thus, one enters the gates of the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*, attaining unimpeded mastery. From the revolution of the letter A, the three bodies (*trikāya*) and four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) are produced, and the Wheel of Dharma is turned.

If a practitioner acts as an ācārya for others, they must first establish the Great Compassion Womb Maṇḍala King and abide in the state of Buddhahood; by assembling these various syllables to form the body, one immediately abides in the state of Buddhahood.
However, when arranging the syllables, they are divided into four layers, each layer containing three types of *namas* (refuge).
The head constitutes the first layer;
the throat constitutes the second layer;
The heart is divided into three parts;
the navel is divided into four parts. A Ā Am Aḥ Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa.

[The seed syllables: Aṅga-ra-ṇa-ma-kha-ra-ṇa-ma-hya-na-ma-baṃ-ka-ja-ṭa-ṇa-na-mo. Regarding the method for arranging these characters:
one should visualize the letter *Ka* from between the brows of the practitioner, at the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*), extending to the right.
They revolve following the movement of the day, causing them to join in a continuous circle;
the four layers are likewise arranged, each uniting and integrating to form the body.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:

“Ka, La, Ṭa, Ta, Pa—through these initial, middle, and final phonemes, augmented by the mutual entry of the categories of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one naturally attains the practice of the bodhicitta, achieving perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and parinirvāṇa.”
These are the fourfold meanings of the initial syllables A, Ā, Am, and Aḥ;
furthermore, the twenty syllables beginning with Ka, Ca, Ṭa, Ta, and Tha represent the intermediate meaning;
and the twelve syllables from I and Ī up to O and Au represent the added meaning of the categories of samādhi.
Furthermore, the twenty characters—yaṅ, raṅ, ṇa, na, ma, up to śa; as well as rwa, nyog, nog, and mog—constitute the meaning of the subsequent characteristics.
Therefore, speaking generally, the natural interpenetration of the marks is further analyzed into three parts:
the head constitutes the first part, which is yellow;
the throat and heart constitute the middle part, which is white;
The navel is the posterior portion, which is black in color.
If the syllable *ka* is used as the wheel, the syllable *kha* is not used;

if the syllable *kha* is used as the wheel, the syllable *ka* is not used. This is called the generation of the bodhicitta, with practice and fruition as the middle, and great quiescence as the end; these are known as the three portions.

Once the ācārya has thus completed the threefold formation of the body, he likewise arranges the maṇḍala and the disciple in the same manner; when these three matters are all accomplished, it is called the Secret Maṇḍala.

If one does not thoroughly comprehend the underlying intent herein, it will be difficult to act in accordance with the aforementioned phenomena; such action cannot be called well-executed, for it is a mere waste of effort and achieves nothing at all.

Furthermore, this method of arranging the syllables is the Great Compassion Womb (Mahākaruṇā-garbha) Triple-layered Secret Maṇḍala. Unless one has personally accumulated the practice of true illumination (*vidyā*) and is worthy of receiving the transmission, it may only be transmitted through mental visualization; it cannot be recorded in writing. Therefore, the Master orally transmitted it as stated in the Sūtra:
"It is simply called the 'Chapter on the Wheel of Syllables' (*Akṣara-cakra-paṭala*)."
The twelve syllables *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* are all scattered outside the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*), arising from flames of light.

Furthermore, the five syllables *aṃ*, *raṃ*, *ṇaṃ*, *naṃ*, and *maṃ* revolve according to the three wheels; they enter into one another spontaneously. This wheel is precisely the meaning of the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).

When the practitioner corresponds in this manner, the arrangement of syllables and the recitation constitute the body of a Vidyādhara; it is no different from the empowerment of the Great Tathāgata Vairocana’s spiritual power. This wheel is also called the Wheel of Causes and Conditions.
When the master, the disciple, and the maṇḍala all likewise arrange these syllables, it is also called the Secret Wheel.
Furthermore, these syllables are the syllables of the heart-mind of all Buddhas, and are thus also called the Mantra Wheel.
As for "wheel" (*cakra*), in the Sanskrit language it is called *akṣaracakra*.
*Akṣaracakra* means that from a single syllable, the letter *a*, many syllables are produced; therefore, it is called a wheel.

The letter A is the very essence of bodhi. Just as Mahāvairocana abides in the essence of the bodhicitta, manifesting in various ways for the universal benefit of all through infinite and boundless transformations, so too does he manifest these traces endlessly; yet in reality, he is eternally quiescent and immovable, without arising or ceasing. It is like a wheel that, though it revolves without end, never wavers from its center.

Because it is immovable, it can govern all capacities for awakening; to move while being without movement is precisely the meaning of the letter A as primordial non-arising. Since there is neither arising nor ceasing, there is neither movement nor regression, yet all letters are produced; these wheels turn endlessly within one another, and this is called the Immovable Wheel.

If an ācārya can thus realize and penetrate the immovable wheel and arrange the various syllables, his very being will naturally manifest such that whatever is expressed by the body is none other than a secret mudrā;
whatever is spoken by the mouth is all a mantra;
and the mind will always abide such that there is nothing that is not a gate of contemplation.
All those who see, hear, touch, or know this shall certainly be destined for unsurpassed bodhi; the merit and benefit they achieve will be true and not in vain.
If one can act in this way, one is identical to Vairocana Tathāgata, performing the work of a Buddha and constantly illuminating the world.
When the ācārya performs recitation, he may visualize the *padmacakra* (wheel of syllables).

Regarding the *padmacakra*: he visualizes the heart of the deity as a luminous orb upon which the letters of the mantra are arranged, revolving and connecting one another, appearing clearly before him.
He visualizes this wheel of syllables like white milk, flowing down in succession into the practitioner’s mouth or onto his crown, continuing without interruption until it completely fills his body.
Within that perfect luminosity is a seed-syllable, which is always clearly manifest, like a flowing stream that is inexhaustible.
When one becomes utterly exhausted from such recitation, one should simply abide in the syllable *A*, the mind of quiescence.
Furthermore, the term "three lakṣas" refers to a number, specifically three hundred thousand recitations.
If the practitioner also beholds the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and mudrās of the *iṣṭadevatā*, they shall perceive the deity within those very seed-syllables and mudrās.

Having thus achieved accomplishment, one is then able to universally arrange all syllables to form one's own body; that is, knowing one's own mind as it truly is, one becomes the body of universal illumination—this is the meaning of "lakṣa."

If one does not practice in such a manner, even if one were to maintain mindfulness for a full ten million lakṣas over the course of a hundred years, success would still not be achieved; how much less so for three lakṣas?
If a practitioner attains equality in the three characteristics:
first, the true characteristic of the body, which is one lakṣa, removes all defilements of the body;
second, the true characteristic of speech, which is two lakṣas, removes all defilements of speech.
Third, the true nature of the mind removes all mental defilements.

Once the three defilements are removed, the three merits arise, and one partially realizes the merits of a Tathāgata. Thus, through the correspondence of these activities, one abides in the bodhicitta precepts; all the pāramitās of the stages are fully perfected because one relies upon the clear prohibitions according to the teachings of the Dharma in which one dwells.
According to one’s vows, the fruit is accomplished, and one should always compassionately protect oneself and others.
The Sūtra says:
"The Lord of Secrets addressed the Buddha, saying:
'How does the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha attain the knowledge of all modes of knowledge?'"
They extensively expound and distribute various paths, proclaiming the wisdom of all-knowledge.
Each speaks in a voice identical to that of others, abiding in various modes of deportment, yet the path to the wisdom of all-knowledge is of a single flavor.
World-Honored One!
For example, the natures of earth, water, fire, wind, and space pervade all places; none of them transcend the gateway of the letter A.
Therefore, Vajrapāṇi asked the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana:
"What is the cause of such wisdom? What is its root?"
"What is its ultimate consummation?
The Buddha told Vajrapāṇi:
"The bodhicitta is the cause, compassion is the root, and skillful means is the ultimate consummation."
Lord of Secrets! What is bodhi?
It is said:
"To know one's own mind as it truly is, it is the single characteristic of the letter A; yet it is neither one nor different.
Furthermore, a sutra says:
"Listen attentively, Vajrapāṇi!"
"Now, I shall explain the dharma-gate for fulfilling the wisdom of all wisdom through the practice of the maṇḍala.

Thus, when the myriad practices are perfected and can no longer be increased, and when the provisional means that respond to sentient beings have exhausted their capacity, this is the source of the three mysteries—the sublime fruit of *amṛta* (ghee). One who knows this supreme reality is named an Ācārya."
Therefore, one should be fully equipped with skillful means and thoroughly understand what the Buddha has taught; thus the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, Guhyakādhipati!
That which is proclaimed by all Buddhas..."
Arrange the various letter-gates; listen with single-minded attention, O Son of the Buddha.
The letter *ka* is at the base of the throat; the letter *kha* is on the upper palate;
the letter *ga* forms the neck; and the letter *gha* is in the throat.
The syllable *ca* is the tongue-root; the syllable *cha* is in the middle of the tongue;
the syllable *ja* is the tip of the tongue; the syllable *jha* is the place where the tongue arises.
The syllable *ṭa* constitutes the shank; one should know that the syllable *ṭha* corresponds to the thigh.
The syllable *Ṇa* is said to be the waist; the syllable *Ṭa* is for sitting at ease.
The syllable *Ta* is the final division; the syllable *Tha* should be known as the abdomen.
The syllable *Na* represents the two hands; the syllable *Dha* is placed on the name as the ribs.
The syllable *Pa* constitutes the back; one should know that the syllable *Pha* is the chest;
the syllable *Ma* is the upper arm; the syllable *Bha* is next, below the arm.
The syllable *Maṃ* dwells at the heart; the syllable *Ya* is the mark of the secret organ.
The syllable RA is named the eye; the syllable LA is the broad forehead.
E and Ī are at the two corners of the eyes; U and Ū are the two lips;
E and Ai are the two ears; O and Au are the two cheeks.
The syllable *Aṃ* is the phrase of bodhi; the syllable *Aḥ* is parinirvāṇa.
Knowing all dharmas thus, the practitioner attains perfect enlightenment.
The provisions for omniscience always abide within his mind.
"World-renowned as All-Knowing, this is called Sarvajñā (Omniscience).
